science.text: The dingo reached Australia about 4,000 years ago. Around the same time, the languages and stone tools of mainland Australia changed, which has led researchers to infer that human contact took place.
Around 4,000 years ago, the Pama-Nyungan language family spread over most of the Australian mainland. In the same period, stone tool technology shifted toward smaller tools.

A 2013 genetic study suggests that Indian and Australian populations mixed well before European contact. The study dated this gene flow to the Holocene, about 4,230 years ago. It is one of the pieces of evidence for contact between India and Australia in this era.

The 2013 study was carried out by the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology. It used large-scale genotyping data from Aboriginal Australians, New Guineans, island Southeast Asians and Indians.

The researchers offered two theories for the gene flow from India. Some Indians may have had contact with people in Indonesia who eventually passed those genes on to Aboriginal Australians. Alternatively, a group of Indians may have migrated all the way to Australia and mixed with the locals directly.

A second kind of genetic evidence is a male Y chromosome lineage called haplogroup C∗. Its most recent common ancestor lived around 5,000 years ago. It has been proposed as another sign of gene flow from India to Australia.

philosophy.text: The Wandjina are cloud and rain spirits in the beliefs of the Wanjina Wunggurr Aboriginal cultural bloc of the Kimberley region in northwestern Australia. Some of the rock art depicting them dates back to about 4,000 years ago.

Alongside the Wandjina, the Wanjina Wunggurr cultural bloc also holds beliefs in Wunngurr, a creator being related to the Rainbow Serpent found in other Aboriginal traditions but understood differently. One aspect of Wunngurr is embodied in a rock python known as Wanjad.

According to research led by Hamish McGowan, the emergence of Wandjina art depicting cloud and rain spirits, dated to 3,800 to 4,000 years ago, coincides with the end of a severe mega-drought and the return of rain to the Kimberley. McGowan suggested the shift might even reflect a cultural collapse, possibly involving a new group replacing the earlier Gwion Gwion artists.

Archaeologist Peter Veth of the University of Western Australia disputed the idea that the shift from Gwion Gwion to Wandjina art reflected a cultural collapse. He pointed out that Kimberley archaeology shows no break in occupation across this transition, and that similar stylistic changes occurred elsewhere in Aboriginal Australia.

culture.text: The dingo reached Australia about 4,000 years ago. Because this arrival came at the same time as other changes on the continent, human contact has been inferred.

Elsewhere in the world the Iron Age followed the Bronze Age, but in Australia indigenous metalworking arrived only with European contact. Aboriginal material culture in this era was therefore not based on metal.

About 4,000 years ago, stone tool technology in Australia changed, with the use of smaller tools. This happened around the same time as the dingo's arrival and the spread of the Pama-Nyungan languages.

A 2013 study by the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology found that Indian and Australian populations mixed well before European contact. It dated this gene flow to the Holocene, about 4,230 years ago.

Researchers offered two theories for the gene flow from India to Aboriginal Australians. Either some Indians had contact with people in Indonesia who passed those genes on, or a group of Indians migrated all the way to Australia and intermingled with the locals directly.

A male Y chromosome lineage called haplogroup C*, with a most recent common ancestor around 5,000 years ago, has also been proposed as evidence of gene flow from India to Australia. It is the second kind of evidence cited alongside the genome-wide SNP data.
